description: We are a team of undergraduate students from Indonesia with backgrounds in Information Systems. Our team combines NASA lunar data (LRO LOLA terrain and SPICE geometry), data analysis, and software development to build Skyline, a tool that shows when lunar landing sites can see the Sun and Earth. Skyline turns complex, siloed data into one integrated, user-friendly experience, from curious learners to mission planners.
summary:
SKYLINE is a web-based lunar landing site navigator for learners, educators and mission planners. At the Moon's south pole the Sun barely rises above the horizon, so a ridge only a few degrees high can block it, and Earth can drop behind the hills for hours or days. That decides whether a lander has solar power and a direct link home.

NASA already has the data to answer this, but it is spread across specialist tools and formats. SKYLINE turns that complex, fragmented data into one clear picture: where the Sun and Earth sit against each site's real terrain horizon, at any moment.

It has three modes. Explore lets anyone fly from the whole Moon down to a polar ridge and stand on it in 3D. Understand is a guided "choose, try, observe, explain" lab for students and educators. Analyze lets mission planners set their requirements, compare sites and find landing dates that meet them.

Under the hood, terrain skylines come from NASA LOLA elevation models and Sun and Earth positions from NASA JPL SPICE. Every number is computed from that data, with its source and assumptions attached.
details:
What it does
SKYLINE answers three questions for a lunar site and time window: Is the Sun in view? Can the site see Earth? How long is the longest blackout? It does this in three experiences:

  • Explore: start from the whole Moon, fly down to a polar ridge, and stand on it in 3D. Watch the Sun and Earth move across a full lunar month and see when the terrain hides them.
  • Understand: a guided lab for students and educators. Pick a question (Can a mountain hide the Sun? Is more light always better? What if we arrive a day later?), predict what happens on a specific date, test it in the 3D model by changing the time or the place, then explain why it happened.
  • Analyze: a workspace for mission planners. Set the mission requirements, landing sites and stay length, compare sites side by side, and find the landing dates that meet every limit. Analyze covers our three south-pole study sites plus the landing sites of other missions, such as Chandrayaan-3, Chang'e and SLIM.

How it works

  1. Terrain: For each site and observer height, we build a 360° terrain skyline at 0.25° azimuth resolution from NASA PGDA LOLA polar DEMs (80 m/px locally, 240 m/px for distant terrain up to 400 km), including lunar curvature.
  2. Ephemeris: NASA JPL NAIF SPICE kernels (DE440, lunar PA/ME frames, leap seconds) provide precise Sun and Earth positions as seen from the site.
  3. Visibility: The Sun is modelled as a finite disk, so partial sunlight is captured. Clearance is the target elevation minus the terrain horizon. Rise/set events are refined with root-finding instead of coarse sampling.
  4. Metrics: Availability fraction, longest blackout and mean visible solar fraction. Every result carries provenance: data hashes, observer, profile and cadence.

Beyond the core challenge

  • Mast placement: tests antenna heights and nearby positions on real terrain, within slope and cable limits, and returns the best trade-offs (Pareto-optimal). In a one-day test at Connecting Ridge on 6 January 2025, a 2 m mast raised Earth visibility from about 36% to about 75%.
  • Relay coverage: compares direct-to-Earth contact with contact through a relay satellite. In six one-day test windows in January 2025, relay assistance covered 100% of the sampled time. At Connecting Ridge on 6 January, direct contact alone covered only 36% of the day, with a longest gap of about 15 hours.
  • Rover reach: a time-dependent graph of where a rover can travel while keeping sunlight and an Earth link.

Benefits and intended impact
Mission planners get a quick, evidence-based way to compare sites and dates before running costly detailed studies. Educators and students get an intuitive way to understand why polar lighting is so unusual. Our goal is to make NASA’s lunar data usable for decisions and learning, not just for specialists.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, TanStack, Tailwind v4, D3/SVG, Three.js, Zod, Vitest.
  • Backend: Go 1.24 (net/http) API orchestration.
  • Science services: Python with NumPy, SciPy, SpiceyPy, Rasterio, pyproj, pymoo, FastAPI and Pydantic.
  • Infrastructure: Docker and Nginx.

Creativity
We combine an educational storytelling layer and a scientific planning engine in one product, with the same physics underneath both. We also go beyond “where is it sunny” to ask how a mast, a relay satellite or a rover changes the answer.

Factors we considered
Scientific honesty matters. Every result states its assumptions and limits. Missing data is never shown as zero. Results are geometric visibility, not certified power output or RF link performance. We also considered accessibility for non-experts, reproducibility through pinned and hashed datasets, and clear units (UTC, degrees, metres, seconds).
